text.en: Ivan the Terrible, the Mughal emperor Akbar and Elizabeth I were contemporaries: from 1558 to 1584 all three reigned at the same time.
While Magellan's expedition circled the globe, Cortés fought the Aztecs. Magellan was killed in April 1521; Tenochtitlan fell that August.
Silver from Potosí (1545) made the Spanish peso the first truly global currency: from 1571, Manila galleons carried it across the Pacific to China.
Some scientists think the 1600 eruption of Peru's Huaynaputina caused the cooling behind Russia's Great Famine of 1601–1603, which helped spark the Time of Troubles.
In 1610 Galileo discovered Jupiter's moons — while in Moscow the Seven Boyars ruled and a Polish garrison entered the city.
Cervantes and Shakespeare died in April 1616 on nearly the same calendar date — but Spain used the Gregorian calendar and England did not, so over a week really separates them.
The last aurochs, the wild ancestor of cattle, died in a Polish forest in 1627 — 14 years after Michael Romanov was elected tsar.
The last confirmed sighting of a dodo was in 1662 — just as Louis XIV was beginning to rebuild Versailles.
The authoritative text of the first Russia–China treaty, Nerchinsk (1689), was in Latin: Jesuit interpreters handled the talks.
In 1564 Ivan Fyodorov printed the Apostol in Moscow, and Shakespeare was born in England. Ivan the Terrible was 33 at the time.
Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547, four years after Copernicus published that the Earth goes round the Sun.
Ivan the Terrible's Oprichnina (1565–1572) and France's St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572) were bloody purges of the same decade.
While False Dmitry I ruled in Moscow (1605–1606), the first part of Don Quixote came out in Madrid.
Five years after the Romanovs came to power (1613), the Thirty Years' War broke out in Europe.
Peter I became tsar in 1682; a year later the Ottomans were stopped at the gates of Vienna. The Europe he would go to learn from had only just held off the Turks.
The last independent Maya kingdom fell only in 1697, 176 years after Tenochtitlan, when Peter the Great was already ruling Russia.
In 1637 a single tulip bulb could cost more than ten years of a skilled craftsman's wages. That was the peak of Dutch tulip mania — the market crashed that same February.
The Thirty Years' War began when officials were thrown out of a window — and survived. Catholics credited the Virgin Mary; Protestants said they landed on a dung heap below Prague Castle.
The most famous rhinoceros in art was drawn by a man who never saw one. Dürer worked from a sketch, adding armour plates and an extra horn — and rhinos were drawn his way for over 200 years.
The first worldwide manhunt in history was for a pirate — and it failed. Henry Every robbed the Mughal emperor's ship in 1695 and vanished with his loot; his fate is unknown.
Indian Ocean pirates were supplied by a New York merchant. Frederick Philipse shipped rum and powder to Madagascar, where Adam Baldridge ran a store for pirates, and took their loot in return.
When Oda Nobunaga first saw the African Yasuke in 1581, he had his skin scrubbed, thinking it was ink. Convinced otherwise, he took Yasuke into service with a stipend and a sword.
In a small town near Seville, hundreds of people bear the surname Japón — "Japan". They are thought to descend from samurai of Hasekura's embassy who reached Spain in 1614 and never went home.
In 1615 a Japanese samurai was made an honorary citizen of Rome. Hasekura Tsunenaga met the pope, but when he got home in 1620 Christianity had been banned in Japan.
Kabuki, where men play every role, was invented by a woman. The dancer Okuni began performing around 1603; in 1629 the shogunate banned women from the stage.
The first European account of Korea was written by a sailor chasing his back pay. Hendrick Hamel spent 13 years stuck in Korea and wrote his report to claim wages from the Dutch East India Company.
In 1602 an Italian drew a world map for the Chinese — and moved the Pacific to the middle. Matteo Ricci did it so China would sit near the centre of the world, as his readers expected.
Shah Jahan's throne reportedly cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal. The Peacock Throne of gold and gems took seven years to make; Nader Shah carried it off from Delhi in 1739.
Legend says the first Ottoman flyer was rewarded with a bag of gold — and then exiled. Sultan Murad IV supposedly decided that a man who could glide across the Bosphorus was too dangerous.
In 1667 the Dutch chose a tiny nutmeg island over Manhattan. Under the Treaty of Breda they kept Run in Indonesia, while the English kept New Amsterdam, which became New York.
The famous "$24 for Manhattan" is a 19th-century conversion. In 1626 the Dutch handed over goods worth 60 guilders; a historian turned that into dollars in 1846.
The Roanoke colony may have been lost because of the Spanish Armada. Governor White sailed home for supplies, but the war kept him away three years — in 1590 he found only CROATOAN carved on a post.
The oldest European object from Australia is a pewter plate. Dirk Hartog nailed it to a post in 1616; 81 years later it was taken to Amsterdam, where it is now in the Rijksmuseum.
Abel Tasman sailed right around Australia without ever seeing it. In 1642–43 he passed far south and east of the mainland, finding Tasmania and New Zealand along the way.
For centuries Europeans searched for Prester John, a legendary Christian king — and concluded he ruled Ethiopia. A Portuguese embassy that arrived in 1520 stayed there six years.
Newton made his greatest discoveries during a plague lockdown. When the plague of 1665 closed Cambridge, he went home to his village and worked on calculus, optics and gravity.
Johannes Kepler spent six years defending his own mother against charges of witchcraft. Katharina Kepler's case dragged on from 1615 to 1621 and ended with her release.
Kepler wrote one of the first works of science fiction — about a journey to the Moon. He finished Somnium around 1608; it was published after his death, in 1634.
The first universities in the Americas are 85 years older than Harvard. San Marcos in Lima and the Royal University of Mexico were founded in 1551; Harvard in 1636.
One of the most accurate pictures of a dodo was painted at the Mughal court. Ustad Mansur painted the bird around 1625; the last dodo was seen in 1662.
The Mughal emperor Jahangir hung a "chain of justice" with 60 bells outside his palace. Any subject could pull it to bring a complaint to the emperor in person.
The Mughal emperor Akbar assembled a library of 24,000 volumes but apparently could not read himself. Books were read aloud to him.
The founder of the Mughal Empire missed melons in India. Babur complained in his memoirs that the country had no good horses, no grapes and no muskmelons.
Japanese tempura came from Portugal. The Portuguese reached Japan in 1543 and brought battered fried food — and the Japanese word "pan" for bread is Portuguese too.
"Isfahan is half the world," Persians said under Shah Abbas. The city's great square, Naqsh-e Jahan, was a polo ground — and its stone goalposts still stand.
The Ottoman admiral Piri Reis drew a map showing the coast of South America in 1513. He wrote that his sources included a map by Columbus that has since been lost.
The first sailors to circle the globe "lost" a day. Returning in 1522, they found their log was one day behind the calendar, although they had kept it without a gap.
Most online maps use a projection from 1569. Gerardus Mercator designed it for sailors, and web maps still use a version of it.
Bombay came to England as a dowry. The Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza married Charles II in 1662, bringing Bombay and Tangier — and she made tea fashionable at court.
Cape Town began as a vegetable garden. In 1652 the Dutch East India Company set up a station to supply passing ships with fresh vegetables and meat on the long voyage to Asia.
Spanish still says "worth a Potosí" for something priceless. The Andean silver city was so famous that Don Quixote tells Sancho "the mines of Potosí" would not be enough to pay him.
The Plains Indians became horse peoples only in the 17th–18th centuries. The Spanish brought horses back to the Americas, and they spread across the Plains after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.
Legend says Copernicus saw his great book on the day he died. The first copy of On the Revolutions was brought to him, already gravely ill, in May 1543.
The Dutch East India Company issued the first shares ever traded on a stock exchange in 1602. Seventeen years later it founded Batavia on Java, today's Jakarta.

Ivan the Terrible did not blind the architects of St Basil's Cathedral. It is a legend: after the church, Postnik Yakovlev worked on the Kremlin's Annunciation Cathedral and built the walls and towers of the Kazan Kremlin.
Ivan the Terrible asked Elizabeth I for asylum in England in case his boyars overthrew him. The queen agreed, provided he paid his own way. Later he even sought to marry her relative Mary Hastings.

The Russian Church split over how many fingers to cross oneself with. Nikon's reform replaced two fingers with three and a double 'hallelujah' with a triple one, and Old Believers saw the number of the beast in the year 1666.
In 1517 both Christendom and Islam changed course: in January the Ottomans took Cairo and soon became masters of Mecca and Medina, and in October Luther published his Ninety-five Theses.
In 1526 two battles fought with cannon redrew the map of Eurasia: in April Babur won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire, and in August Sultan Suleiman crushed Hungary at Mohács.

St Basil's Cathedral and the Süleymaniye Mosque were going up at the same time: Sinan built the mosque in 1550–1557 and Moscow raised the cathedral in 1555–1561, so for a couple of years both were building sites.
St Basil's Cathedral is more than 70 years older than the Taj Mahal: it was consecrated in 1561, and work on the Agra mausoleum began only in 1632.
In 1571 Spain was busy at both ends of its empire: in June it founded Manila in the Philippines, and in October it joined its allies in destroying the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto.
Two and a half months after the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre a new star blazed in the sky. Tycho Brahe spotted it on 11 November 1572 and showed the heavens could change: it was a supernova.
The last supernova seen in our galaxy blazed five years before Galileo turned a telescope to the sky. Kepler's star appeared in 1604, and no Milky Way supernova has been reliably seen since.

Galileo was born three days before Michelangelo died, and Newton in the year Galileo died: Galileo on 15 February 1564, Michelangelo dying on the 18th, and Newton on Christmas Day 1642 by England's Julian calendar.

The last months of 1600 shaped two island nations: in October the Battle of Sekigahara opened the way to 265 years of Tokugawa rule in Japan, and on 31 December Elizabeth I chartered the East India Company.
Europeans first landed in Australia after Don Quixote was published. Cervantes' novel came out in 1605; the Dutchman Willem Janszoon reached the Australian coast aboard the Duyfken in 1606.
In 1648, as Europe signed the Peace of Westphalia, the Cossack Semyon Dezhnev became the first European to sail the strait between Asia and America — 80 years before Bering.
Raphael painted a memorial fresco for an elephant. Hanno, Pope Leo X’s white pet, lived in Rome for two years; when he died in 1516, the pope buried him in the Vatican and wrote his epitaph himself.

After the elephant’s success, Portugal’s king decided to send the pope a rhinoceros too. But early in 1516 the ship sank off Italy and the chained rhino drowned: the very animal Dürer had immortalised.

Rats once had a lawyer. In 1522 they were tried at Autun in Burgundy for ruining barley, and the jurist Barthélemy de Chasseneuz won a delay: the rats could not attend court, since cats lay in wait along the way.

The world’s largest insurance market began in a coffee house. In 1680s London, sailors and merchants drank coffee at Edward Lloyd’s, heard the shipping news and insured cargoes on the spot: that was Lloyd’s.
The Ottoman sultan Murad IV banned coffee on pain of death. Contemporaries said he walked Istanbul at night in disguise, catching offenders himself, along with smokers and drinkers.
The Italian pomodoro means “golden apple”: the botanist Mattioli used the name in 1544, perhaps because the first tomatoes in Europe were yellow. “Tomato” comes from the Aztec word tomatl.
Cacao beans were money for the Aztecs, and they were counterfeited. Spanish chroniclers described fakes: the insides were removed and the empty husks filled with earth or wax.
Theologians once argued over whether chocolate broke a fast. In 1662 Cardinal Brancaccio ruled that “liquids do not break the fast”, and chocolate stayed on the menu.
The traveller Thomas Coryat brought the fork to England after seeing it in Italy in 1608. His countrymen mocked him as “Furcifer”, fork-bearer, which in Latin also meant rascal.

The flush toilet was invented by Elizabeth I’s godson, the poet John Harington. He installed one at home and reportedly another for the queen at Richmond Palace, but the much-mocked idea was forgotten for two centuries.
In 17th-century Sweden a coin could weigh almost 20 kg. Copper plates were worth their weight in metal, so large payments went by cart. No wonder Sweden issued Europe’s first banknotes.

In 1685 soldiers in New France were paid in playing cards. When the pay ship from Paris was late, the intendant cut up cards, signed them and issued them as money; they circulated in Canada for decades.
The wig craze began with a bald patch. Louis XIII lost his hair early and took to wearing a wig in the 1620s; courtiers followed, and under Louis XIV a full wig became essential male dress.

High heels were made for men. Persian horsemen used them to grip their stirrups, and after Shah Abbas’s embassy to Europe in 1599 aristocrats copied the style. Louis XIV allowed red heels only at court.

The Mayflower Pilgrims hurried ashore at Plymouth partly because of beer. Governor Bradford wrote that supplies were running low, “especially our beer”, and the crew were saving the rest for the voyage home.

Russia’s first tea arrived in 1638 with the envoy Vasily Starkov, a gift to Tsar Michael from a Mongol khan. Starkov tried to refuse the “useless” leaves and asked for sables instead, but took 4 poods of tea.

The great astronomer Tycho Brahe wore a metal nose. He lost part of his own in a 1566 duel with a kinsman, reportedly after a quarrel over mathematics. Tests on his remains suggest the prosthesis was brass, not the gold or silver of legend.
Tycho Brahe kept a tame elk that, so the story goes, was killed by beer. Taken to a banquet at another nobleman's castle, the animal drank too much, fell down the stairs and died.

The most accurate pre-telescope sky survey came from a man who never looked through a telescope. Tycho Brahe died in 1601, eight years before Galileo turned one skywards, yet his data let Kepler find the laws of planetary motion.

1543 overturned ideas about both the heavens and the body. Copernicus published that the Earth goes round the Sun, and Vesalius the first accurate human anatomy based on dissection rather than ancient books.

An Italian doctor spent 30 years weighing himself, his food and everything that left his body. Sitting in a weighing chair, Santorio Santorio found that his excretions weighed less than his meals: the rest escaped unseen in breath and sweat.

The man who wrote the laws of motion also worked as a detective. As Warden of the Royal Mint, Newton went to taverns in disguise, interrogated witnesses and in 1699 sent the master counterfeiter William Chaloner to the gallows.

The founder of classical physics was a devoted alchemist. Newton left an estimated million words of alchemical manuscripts and seriously sought the philosopher's stone; John Maynard Keynes, who bought the papers, called him 'the last of the magicians'.

Newton's Principia nearly went unpublished because of a book about fish. The Royal Society had spent its budget on a lavish History of Fishes that did not sell, so Edmond Halley paid for the Principia himself, and got his salary in copies of the fish book.
Edmond Halley, of comet fame, also went diving in the Thames. In 1691 he designed a diving bell topped up with barrels of fresh air, and stayed under the water for more than an hour and a half.

Galileo probably never did his famous Leaning Tower experiment. It is known only from his pupil's account, while Simon Stevin had already dropped balls from a church tower in Delft in 1586 and seen them land together.

Cells are named after monks' rooms. Robert Hooke looked at cork under a microscope and saw tiny chambers like monastery cells. Samuel Pepys sat up until 2 a.m. reading his Micrographia and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read.

The first bacteria were found in a man's own mouth. In 1683 Leeuwenhoek examined plaque from his teeth and from two old men who had never cleaned theirs, and saw crowds of 'animalcules' moving about 'very prettily'.
Microbes were discovered by a draper. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never went to university; he ground lenses to count threads in cloth, and ended up with the best microscopes in the world.
For centuries Europeans ate Egyptian mummies as medicine. Apothecaries sold powdered 'mummia' for bruises and illness, and King Francis I of France was said to carry some with him at all times.

The Mayflower Pilgrims did not wear black with buckled hats. Black was for Sundays; everyday clothes were coloured, and buckles came into fashion only in the late 17th century; the image was invented by 19th-century artists.
Galileo probably never dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Only his pupil Viviani told the story, decades later; Galileo himself never describes it, so it was likely a thought experiment.
No apple hit Newton on the head. He himself said he saw one fall in his garden and wondered why it always dropped straight down; the bump on the head was added later.
No one was burned at Salem. Of the 20 people executed, 19 were hanged, and the elderly Giles Corey was pressed to death with stones for refusing to enter a plea.
Ivan IV's nickname Grozny meant 'formidable' or 'awe-inspiring' rather than 'terrible' in the modern sense; the English word 'terrible' once meant the same, but its sense has drifted.

The croissant was not invented to celebrate the 1683 victory over the Ottomans at Vienna. That legend only appears in the 20th century, and Austrian crescent-shaped kipferl were baked long before the siege.
The monk Dom Pérignon did not invent champagne; he tried to get rid of the bubbles. Fizz was a fault in Champagne wine, bursting bottles in cellars, and he worked to prevent it.

Magellan did not sail round the world: he was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage; of five ships and about 270 men, one ship and 18 men made it back to Spain.
Ninja did not wear black suits. The image comes from kabuki theatre, where stagehands dressed in black to be 'invisible'; real spies dressed like ordinary people.
